ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.contribution: supplies mandatory first-year academic writing, source evaluation, development planning and civic collaboration

BENBUSI112.name: Accounting & Corporate Finance
BENBUSI112.contribution: Directly supplies Introduces financial accounting, management accounting and investment appraisal, including accounting's social role and accountability implications. Students record transactions, prepare and interpret financial statements, and analyze performance and financing. The course then examines costing, pricing, budgeting, organizational control and sustainable management accounting. Investment decisions are evaluated using accounting and discounted-cash-flow measures. A case study analyzes the misuse of an accounting principle and its financial-statement effects.

BENBUSI211.name: Business & Economy in the Age of AI
BENBUSI211.contribution: Directly supplies Examines AI's business, economic and societal implications without requiring a technical background. AI foundations and limitations lead into applications across enterprise functions and industries, labour-market change, productivity, innovation, market structure and inequality. Governance, corporate responsibility, regulation and future scenarios connect technological developments to institutional choices. Students analyze business cases and competing scholarly arguments, then investigate a country's AI readiness, workforce, regulation and industrial policy.

BENBUSI312.name: Money, Banking & Finance
BENBUSI312.contribution: Directly supplies Examines financial markets and institutions, including the pricing of bonds, stocks and derivatives, interest rates and their risk and term structure, commercial-bank balance sheets and performance, financial structure and regulation, banking fragility and financial crises, central banks, money creation and monetary policy. Students apply algebraic and graphical analysis to financial and monetary problems. In the Stanford Banking Game they manage a simulated bank, analyse performance in Excel dashboards, forecast financial statements, and make evidence-based decisions about loans, deposits, capital, liquidity and risk. A small research project extends a selected financial or monetary research article through additional literature, a case study or updated evidence.

BENECON111.name: Introduction to Economics
BENECON111.contribution: Directly supplies Introduces microeconomic principles and short-run macroeconomic analysis. The microeconomic component examines supply and demand, strategic interaction, consumer choice, production, costs and competitive markets. The macroeconomic component introduces output, unemployment and inflation, then relates goods and financial markets through the IS-LM model. Students use algebra and graphs to explain economic behaviour and apply models to economic issues.

BENECON211.name: International Macroeconomics
BENECON211.contribution: Directly supplies Examines short-, medium- and long-run macroeconomic dynamics and policy, including international dimensions. Students study goods, financial and labour markets, inflation and unemployment, economic growth, expectations and the open economy. IS-LM and IS-LM-PC models connect markets and policy effects. Algebraic and graphical analysis and interpretation of macroeconomic indicators support the evaluation of economic developments and fiscal and monetary policy.

BENECON212.name: Microeconomics & Behavior
BENECON212.contribution: Directly supplies Develops microeconomic theory through consumer behaviour, imperfectly competitive markets and economy-wide allocation. Students examine choice under uncertainty, non-egoistic preferences and cognitive limitations, then monopoly, strategic behaviour and labour and capital markets. General equilibrium, efficiency, externalities and government complete the analysis. Algebraic problem-solving and graphical analysis are connected to the interpretation and evaluation of research papers.

BENECON311.name: Public Economics
BENECON311.contribution: Directly supplies Examines government intervention through the efficiency and equity effects of public policy. Market failure, public goods and externalities provide foundations for studying public production, collective choice, spending and taxation. Health, education, welfare and social insurance illustrate expenditure and redistribution questions. Students apply economic models, interpret data and graphs, evaluate research and develop a research proposal and paper.

BENECON312.name: Econometrics
BENECON312.contribution: Directly supplies Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.

BENECON314.name: Behavioral Economics
BENECON314.contribution: Directly supplies This course integrates insights from psychology into economic theory to better understand how people make decisions. Learn how actual behavior deviates from the predictions of traditional economic models due to biases, heuristics, and framing. Through experiments, students will deepen their understanding of decision-making and its implications for economic theory and practice.

BENENTR211.name: Marketing & Consumer Engagement
BENENTR211.contribution: complements economic consumer/firm analysis through consumer psychology, brand strategy and primary/secondary customer evidence

BENENTR212.name: Strategy & Digital Transformation
BENENTR212.contribution: complements economic study of firms and technological change through strategy, business models and responsible digital transformation; no industrial-economics equivalence

BENENTR311.name: Market Research
BENENTR311.contribution: complements empirical firm/consumer inquiry with planning and conducting customer research, analysing findings and presenting business recommendations; no unsupported named techniques

BENENTR312.name: International Business & Governance
BENENTR312.contribution: Directly supplies Examines how international trade, globalization and political, sociocultural and technological forces shape firms' cross-border decisions. Economic foundations include trade theories, foreign direct investment, foreign exchange and the monetary system. Students analyze governance, responsibility and trade-policy conflicts, investigate an international-business question, and develop an evidence-based market-entry strategy covering country attractiveness and business functions. A tariff case applies game theory to stakeholder choices and negotiation.

BENGATE101.name: Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations
BENGATE101.contribution: complements financial decisions through venture funding, finance/operations planning and business-model appraisal; supplies the formal prerequisite for banking

BENGATE102.name: Research Methods & Statistics
BENGATE102.contribution: Directly supplies Introduces empirical research design and statistical analysis, followed by a substantial student research project. Students study operationalization, measurement quality, sampling, surveys and experimental and nonexperimental designs, then descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression. R and R Commander support data display and analysis. Project teams develop instruments and a research plan, collect and analyze data, and report results under explicit research-ethics and privacy requirements.

BENLEAD112.name: Leadership Communication
BENLEAD112.contribution: complements collective-policy inquiry through leadership rhetoric, ethical public communication and an interview-based advisory report

BENLEAD311.name: Psychology of Organizations & Leadership
BENLEAD311.contribution: complements institutional collective-action inquiry through power, motivation, teams, organisational change and systematic review of organisational research

DISARIN211.name: Decision-making in AI
DISARIN211.contribution: directly supplies Bayesian probability, expected utility and Markov/sequential decisions under uncertainty; it is not an optimisation-methods course

DISCOMP212.name: Database Management Systems
DISCOMP212.contribution: Directly supplies Introduces relational database management systems and SQL. Covers relational database theory, authorization, normalization and query processing.

DISDATA111.name: Introduction to Data Science
DISDATA111.contribution: Directly supplies Introduces data analysis and visualization in R through practical work with tabular, textual and spatial data. Students import, clean, transform and join data, explore patterns, and construct visualizations using tidy-data principles and the grammar of graphics. Web scraping and basic programming functions extend the workflow. A student research project applies these tools to a question using data from a field of interest.

DISDATA211.name: Machine Learning
DISDATA211.contribution: Directly supplies Introduces statistical learning for understanding data and predicting outcomes. Students study regression and classification, model accuracy, resampling, regularization, nonlinear models, trees, support vector machines and unsupervised learning. Practical assignments evaluate methods on real data using R or Python. Projects emphasize informative predictor construction, test-set prediction, appropriate model choice and clear reporting of results and limitations.

DISGATE101.name: Introduction to Programming
DISGATE101.contribution: Directly supplies Introduces computational problem-solving and programming in Python. Students develop structured programs using branching, iteration, functions and data collections, then progress to recursion, exception handling and object-oriented programming with inheritance. Elements of logic, sets and enumeration support computational reasoning. Exercises and projects require students to write, trace, test, debug and explain programs that solve problems of moderate complexity.

DISGATE102.name: Mathematical Methods
DISGATE102.contribution: Directly supplies Develops single-variable calculus and related mathematical tools for modelling scientific problems. Functions, limits and differentiation lead to optimization, Taylor series, complex numbers, integration and differential equations. Students solve problems analytically and with Mathematica, including numerical approximation. A project implements, analyzes and adapts a dynamic model, requiring interpretation of its behaviour and explanation of the computational results.

DISMATH211.name: Linear Algebra
DISMATH211.contribution: Directly supplies Develops linear algebra from systems of equations and matrix operations to vector spaces, linear transformations, eigenvalues and orthogonality. Students study least-squares approximation, symmetric matrices, quadratic forms and singular value decomposition. Applications include discrete signals, difference equations, Markov chains, dynamical systems, graphics and principal component analysis. Mathematica exercises teach computer-algebra approaches to larger problems alongside analytical problem-solving.

DISMATH213.name: Computational & Numerical Methods
DISMATH213.contribution: directly supplies numerical mathematical modelling, root finding, integration, differential equations and stability/error analysis for quantitative financial and economic modelling

DISMATH214.name: Advanced Calculus
DISMATH214.contribution: Directly supplies Extends elementary calculus to multiple dimensions and differential equations, including complex‑valued functions. Uses computer algebra software to deepen analytical skills for science and data analysis applications.

DISMATH314.name: Probability & Statistics
DISMATH314.contribution: Directly supplies Provides a rigorous introduction to probability and mathematical statistics, from probability spaces and random variables to multivariate distributions and statistical inference. Students study estimation, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests and maximum-likelihood methods, followed by an introduction to Bayesian reasoning. Mathematica simulations verify analytical results. A substantial project implements and compares random-sampling algorithms, including inverse sampling, accept-reject sampling and Gibbs sampling.

ENSDELT312.name: Governance of Sustainability
ENSDELT312.contribution: Directly supplies Analyzes sustainability as a problem of collective decision-making involving governments, markets and civil society. Concepts of institutions, power, participation, justice and problem complexity frame competing technological and systemic responses. Structured cases examine food, freshwater, energy and climate mitigation. Students apply governance frameworks to a Zeeland issue, consult relevant organizations or experts, and produce policy advice or an evaluation assessing effectiveness, feasibility and stakeholder interests.

GOSGATE102.name: Law, Society & Justice
GOSGATE102.contribution: complements institutional economic policy through law/society, constitutional/public-law foundations and socio-legal reasoning

GOSLAWJ111.name: Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
GOSLAWJ111.contribution: complements the evaluation of public economic institutions with concrete rights systems, justice arguments and legal limits

GOSPHIL212.name: Ethics
GOSPHIL212.contribution: Directly supplies Studies moral reasoning through historical and contemporary ethical theories and close philosophical reading. Utilitarianism, consequentialism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics lead into Nietzsche's genealogy, Murdoch's account of goodness and Nagel's treatments of value, perspective, death and meaning. Reflection and research essays require interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.

GOSPOLI111.name: Introduction to Political Philosophy
GOSPOLI111.contribution: Directly supplies Surveys political thought from classical antiquity to contemporary debates, including European and non-European thinkers. Students examine views of human nature, society, rights and authority in their historical contexts and compare their proposed solutions with current political problems. Close study of original texts, an individual essay and a group project developing a coherent political philosophy connect historical interpretation to normative argument.

GOSPOLI112.name: Foundations of Comparative Politics
GOSPOLI112.contribution: Directly supplies Introduces empirical comparison of political systems, with democracy, democratization and autocratization as central concerns. Students study political institutions, rules, actors and behaviour, including parties, elections, participation, polarization, interest groups and policy. Research exercises operationalize and measure democracy using V-Dem data and compare academic literature-search tools. A qualitative or quantitative research memo answers a theoretically grounded comparative-politics question through empirical analysis.

GOSPOLI311.name: European Union Politics
GOSPOLI311.contribution: Directly supplies Studies EU institutions, political actors, integration and policymaking, linking formal rules to current political issues. Students analyze representation, legitimacy, interests, agenda setting, decision-making and implementation. A substantial empirical project examines European Parliament committee amendments, connecting MEP ideology and possible interest-group influence to amendment activity. Students develop a project plan, code amendments, assess salience and trace legislative processes.

GOSPOLI312.name: Public Policy Analysis
GOSPOLI312.contribution: Directly supplies Investigates public policy in the context of globalization. Uses a case study on sugar to examine policy‑making phases and alternative conceptualisations across national and international arenas. Students write policy memos.

GOSPOLI313.name: Peace & Conflict
GOSPOLI313.contribution: complements institutions and inequality inquiry through conflict, structural causes, identity, rights and evidence-based peacebuilding policy briefs

GOSSOCI111.name: Introduction to Sociology
GOSSOCI111.contribution: Directly supplies Introduces sociological reasoning through classical theories, their historical settings and perspectives that address exclusions from the discipline. Students connect solidarity, modernity, identity, social boundaries, networks and stratification to race, gender, migration and inequality in education and work. An individual analysis applies a course concept to contemporary social life without original data collection. A group paper develops a sociological question and analyzes a social problem using theory and academic literature.

GOSSOCI212.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
GOSSOCI212.contribution: Directly supplies Develops qualitative inquiry from research design and preparation through data collection, management, analysis and dissemination. Students examine methodological foundations, ethics, positionality and reflexivity alongside interviews, focus groups, ethnography, documentary and visual approaches. Coding, thematic interpretation and NVivo support analysis. Research teams formulate a question, collect and analyze qualitative evidence, and report their methodological decisions, findings and limitations in staged assignments.

GOSSOCI311.name: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
GOSSOCI311.contribution: Directly supplies Focuses on civil society through critical, neo-functionalist and decolonial social theory. Students examine social trust, capital, hegemony, public spheres, solidarity, social movements and civil repair across political and regional contexts. An experience report relates personal engagement or observation to course concepts. An individual research project uses theoretical and empirical sources to analyze a civil-society organization, movement, initiative or related phenomenon.

HCBPSYC211.name: Statistics & Experimental Methods
HCBPSYC211.contribution: Directly supplies Develops experimental-design knowledge and practical statistical analysis for health and behavioural research. Students choose, fit, diagnose and interpret multivariable models, comparing means, analyzing categorical outcomes and studying latent constructs. R, primarily through R Commander, supports repeated practical exercises; SPSS is an optional alternative. Data-analysis papers and a poster connect research questions and hypotheses to appropriate models, assumption checks, substantive interpretation and APA reporting.

MCCCOMM311.name: Persuasive Communication
MCCCOMM311.contribution: complements policy implementation with framing, persuasion and community-based sustainable-behaviour projects; not a generic macroeconomic or policy-economics substitute

alignment.rationale: Both develop reflective competence assessment, study/career choices and development actions. UCR also includes writing, source research and civic collaboration.
Both study financial statements, accounting techniques, costs and organisational control. UCR additionally includes corporate investment appraisal.

Both examine economic power, market structure and societal risks in data/AI economies. Tilburg specifically models data intermediaries, political participation and belief formation; UCR spans enterprise, labour and industrial-policy effects.

Both analyse financial contracts, pricing and investment risk. Tilburg adds dedicated capital-budgeting/CAPM/cost-of-capital foundations; UCR also centres banks, monetary policy and institutional risks.
Both use models of consumers, firms and competitive or imperfect markets. UCR also introduces macroeconomics; the course is counted only once.

Both examine open-economy models, international financial relationships and macroeconomic policy. Tilburg centres exchange-rate theories and monetary systems; UCR spans additional short- and long-run macroeconomic questions.
Both study imperfect competition, strategic firm behaviour, market power and efficiency. Tilburg gives a more dedicated oligopoly, entry, vertical-contract and innovation model sequence.
Both evaluate government intervention, redistribution, public goods and economic policy with models and evidence. Their selected empirical applications differ.

Both develop regression and instrumental-variable estimation for empirical economic research. UCR uses Stata, GLS and Monte Carlo illustration; Tilburg uses R and prepares for time-series/panel methods.

Both study trade theories, cross-border economic relationships and trade-policy conflicts. Tilburg develops calibrated quantitative trade models; UCR applies trade and governance reasoning to international firm decisions.

Both import, manipulate and visualise data in R and use programming functions. Tilburg additionally centres numerical optimisation and economic/stochastic simulation; UCR develops empirical data workflows.

Both develop Python programs, data structures, control flow and analytical problem solving. Tilburg has a shorter economic simulation/data focus; UCR also develops recursion and object-oriented programming.
Both develop calculus and mathematical techniques for modelling and optimisation. Tilburg applies these to economics; UCR includes differential-equation and scientific dynamic-model work.

Both study probability distributions, estimation, confidence intervals and tests. UCR develops more mathematical and Bayesian/simulation methods; Tilburg centres economic applications and Excel/basic R.

Both analyse environmental policy instruments, actors and institutional implementation. UCR centres governance, participation and policy advice; Tilburg adds resource-allocation models, valuation and dynamic environmental economics.

Both develop normative arguments about justice and responsible choices. Tilburg explicitly combines distributive justice and markets with reasoning errors and scientific method; UCR studies a wider range of ethical theories.

analysis: Closest is a substantial economic response: micro/macro, public/behavioural economics, econometrics, finance, probability, calculus, data, Python and linear algebra. Consumer research, marketing, international business/trade and digital strategy serve specific firm/market applications, not general breadth. Replaced product design and organisational psychology with Python and linear algebra to strengthen its methods rather than claim business administration as economics.

Public/institutional economics has a distinct purpose: institutions, justice, inequality and collective policy decisions anchored by economic models and empirical analysis. Legal foundations, comparative politics, sociology/qualitative inquiry, rights, governance, organisational and communicative implementation each have specified roles. Replaced constitutional law with its foundational law/society course to repair the unmet prerequisite without fabricating access, and replaced American Century research with actual Public Policy Analysis.

Financial option makes actual market/banking and quantitative modelling central: accounting, micro/macro, econometrics, probability, linear algebra, calculus, numerical solutions, Python, relational data and Bayesian/sequential decision methods. Replaced digital strategy with numerical mathematics. Probabilistic Decision-making in AI is not an optimisation course. Pairwise differences of 105, 30 and 105 credits each way change priorities and pass the four-course floor.

All forty-two active course contributions were reviewed. Description-only Econometrics receives full OLS/GLS/IV, tests, Stata and empirical-paper consideration; Advanced Calculus, SQL databases, Behavioral Economics, Strategy, Market Research and Public Policy Analysis receive their actual described scope. Market Research supports gathering/analysing customer evidence but not invented named methods. Money and Banking provides contracts, pricing/risk, financial institutions and simulated-bank analysis, not merely personal finance. No absent outline is treated as academic absence.

Six original offering conflicts and one missing constitutional prerequisite are repaired under actual current covered semesters, with five subject substitutions for specific academic reasons. All plans have 24 unique courses, four each semester, 180 EC, PPD in year one and six or more advanced courses. Mathematics precedes formal dependent mathematics; data precedes machine learning; research foundations precede empirical inquiry. No old offering or unprovided term is restored.

Sixteen partial relationships and eleven dedicated gaps cover every external component once and every selected UCR course once. Data Science has a real R-programming/data-workflow relationship; the old no-separate-R-course blank missed that substance. Microeconomics is better placed with Industrial Economics than treating behavioural experiments as Game Theory. Statistics uses the stronger mathematical probability course. Trade is grounded in actual trade theory/foreign investment/monetary and tariff content with quantitative-depth limits. Governance/Environment is a bounded environmental-policy relationship, not identical resource economics. Dedicated theory/history/thesis/communication gaps remain. Optional independent research remains additional to scheduled credits.
